title: The Princess and the Pea
alt: Once we've fully explored this space, we can start varying the number of princesses.
transcript:
[At the top of the panel is a gradated line with arrows at both ends indicating that it extends indefinitely. The middle gradation is a thick line labelled:] 1:1 mattress-to-pea ratio
[Label at the left of the line:] Many mattresses per pea
[Label at the right of the line:] Many peas per mattress

[Below the line are five pictures, showing various images, each with a Jill-like princess in a pink dress. From left to right, they are:
The princess on top of a mountain of mattresses with an arrow indicating a green pea being inserted somewhere in the distance
The princess waving at the top of a pile of several dozen mattresses on a bed with an arrow indicating a pea being inserted at the bottom of the pile
The princess on one bed with an arrow indicating a pea being inserted under the mattress
The princess eating a bowl of peas on the same bed:
The princess on a bed on a mountain of peas which are spilling on to the top of the mattress.]

[The second image, with the princess sitting on top of several dozen mattresses with one pea, is circled.]
[Label pointing to the second image:] Existing Hans Christian Andersen story
[Arrows point to the other four images, with the following label:] Potential sequels/reboots
explanation:
This comic references the  fairy tale , in which a princess's claim to royal blood is tested by having her sleep atop twenty es and twenty , with a single  hidden underneath them. If she is sensitive enough to notice the small lump of the pea through the stack of bedding, it will somehow prove that she is a true princess, and she will be permitted to marry the prince. Randall imagines extending the story into a , adding many sequels and reimaginings by varying the number of mattresses and peas. Randall has previously shown his dislike of movie sequels.

The scenarios depicted range from a high mattress:pea  on the left to a high pea:mattress ratio on the right. In the middle, the princess (here portrayed by a version of Jill in a pink princess dress) sleeps on a single mattress concealing a single pea. This might be considered a slightly more reasonable test of sensitivity than that in the original story. On the far left there is a mountain of mattresses with a single pea concealed amongst them, which would not be a particularly effective test since there's no guarantee that the princess is sleeping anywhere near the pea, never mind on top of it. On the far right, she has a single mattress on a sea of peas, which would, again, be fairly useless, since the peas would be clearly visible. This would defeat the purpose of the test as the princess would know the peas are there and could just claim to have felt them even if she didn't. In the second right image, the princess has a normal bed with a single mattress, and has a bowl of peas, which she is eating. Since the pea(s) in the story are dried peas, eating them as they are would be inadvisable, but this perhaps suggests that, with enough peas, the princess would cook them, and would therefore not continue feeling them under her, subverting the test entirely. Obtaining the sea of mattresses and peas shown on the furthest ends of the graph would be a very difficult task (not to mention cleaning them up), and would be rather a lot of effort for a (fairly useless) task.

The title text takes things a step further by proposing to change another variable: the number of princesses sleeping in the bed (whether together or separately is unclear). This could provide a storyline where the real princess is discovered from a set of false princesses. Alternatively, it could result in multiple real princesses being discovered, leading to a  marriage for the prince, which would be unusual for a European fairy tale. Or the princesses might get along famously and decide to do without the prince.

The existing comic varies the mattress:pea ratio while keeping the number of princesses fixed at one, but the title text's proposal implies that we could also vary the princess:mattress and princess:pea ratios at the same time. The effects of different combinations of these variable ratios could be illustrated by adding two further axes to the comic, expanding it into three dimensions; or, in just two dimensions, a version of a  that plots the three sub-proportions of mattresses, peas and princesses compared to the sum total of mattresses+peas+princesses.
